This is exactly the wrong conclusion to draw from this chart. The three sets of colored dots corresponding to three distinct economic regimes actually show very clearly why.

Blue (1958–81), beta=0.93: inflation-dominated and Fisher equation does the work: 10y and inflation (expectations) move 1 for 1.

Orange (1982–2000), beta=1.45: Volcker disinflation plus a large, then-compressing term premium. Yields started far above NGDP and fell as inflation was wrung out. 

Green (2001–25), beta=0.30: This is the present. Once inflation was anchored, most of the x-axis variation was cyclical or a modest change in real growth. Yields barely tracked it. 

The yellow dot or today’s macro condition is “exactly where it should be” only if we believed that all three regimes are continuously part of the same. They are not. 

Either we remain in the Green regime, where inflation expectations remain anchored even if temporarily elevated, in which case 10y is too high. Or we are part of the Orange or even Blue regime and inflation expectations are becoming unanchored, in which case 10y is too low. 

I think we are potentially at an inflection point or watershed moment. Policy decisions in the coming months can tip us over into a treacherous and costly inflationary regime or keep us in the more benign regime even if a bit warmer for comfort.

Many fields spend enormous energy on prestige allocation. 

Judging prize winners, refereeing papers, organizing seminars, deciding who gets tenure. Mathematicians are not highly paid; their compensation is largely in prestige and in the intellectual enjoyment of the work.

Prestige allocation is very important. I am not demeaning this. Poor prestige allocation leads to warped incentives and a field of work getting benchmaxxed away from its underlying social goal. (China's cash-for-publications policy, which was ended in 2020, was a classic case of this.) It is appropriate for a field to spend of energy getting prestige allocation right, the same way it's important for a company to spend extra time and energy to make sure that capable employees are recognized and rewarded.

So why are people reacting badly to the mathematics letter? Put aside the Navier-Stokes drama, we all agree that was scandalous. That didn't need a letter. This letter is about much more than that: AI Labs, you are breaking our prestige allocation structures. Who do we give prizes to? Who should get tenure? Who will give the seminars? How do we continue to motivate young mathematicians? We carefully calibrated these systems, and you are breaking them in the search for glory in a different prestige system than our own. Show some respect for the way we do things.

The reason why tech people are reacting badly to this, I suspect, is because programmers—the backbone of the tech industry—just went through this. The programming prestige allocation has already been toppled. 10x programmers got displaced by 20-year-old tokenmaxxers and agent orchestrators. If you spent your career memorizing the minutiae of SQL query planners, that is now an encyclopedic party trick. Everything is changing, and the answer has been a resounding: get the fuck over it. Nobody else cares. Programming serves human goals, not programmer prestige hierarchies.

It is painful. But I think this is the right answer. Programmers will survive, and so will mathematicians.

Mathematics does not exist for mathematicians. It exists for humanity. If mathematics needs to adapt to AI, and if that adaptation will be painful and chaotic, if it will force the field and its social structures to rapidly reassemble, then the sooner the better.

It is not technology's job to genuflect to our existing social structures. It has always and forever been the job of social structures to adapt to technology. Any answer to the contrary—to the printing press, to industrialization, to television, to the internet, and now to AI—correctly resides in the dustbins of history.

BREAKING: Earnings for VLCC supertankers on the benchmark Middle East-to-China route are up to nearly $800,000 per day, an all-time high.

Rates have more than doubled over the last 2 months.

At the same time, the rate for a VLCC charter from the US Gulf to Asia is up to a record ~$29.5 million per voyage, before additional war-risk costs and fees for potential delays.

The surge has been driven by fewer vessels willing to transit the Strait of Hormuz, sharply reducing available shipping capacity.

As a result, alternative routes keep each tanker at sea for more time, further reducing the number of vessels available.

Looking ahead, earnings for VLCCs are estimated to stay above $100,000 a day into next year, more than double historical levels, which rarely exceeded $45,000 a day, according to Kpler.

Inflation is back.

Love the depth in this playbook.

Just remember, trading 24/7 isn't a good thing in the long term.

There’s definitely such a thing as trading exhaustion and decision fatigue. When you trade for too long, your decisions eventually get sloppier, and it gets harder to judge risk properly.

If you've been losing, you start hesitating on setups you’d normally take.

If you've been winning, the opposite can happen. You start sizing up, chasing more, and it's never enough.

Sometimes the best course of action is to touch grass for a few days.

You come back calmer, less attached to your previous positions, and usually much better at deciding what to trade.

Markets are open 24/7.
There will always be opportunities.

Japan is awesome for so many reasons but one thing they do over there that I really love is how they rate restaurants via their native eating site Tablelog

On Google it feels like a good place get 5 stars and a 3 star review means it’s pretty meh, and there’s not a whole lot of discernment or delineation (like is a 4.8 star really THAT much better than a 4.4 star?)

In Japan, they treat 3 stars as pretty good and anything above that is exceptional

A 5 star review is very rare and a restaurant with an average rating over like 3.5 actually means something, and there’s a HUGE difference between like 3.5 and 3.9

l dunno, I just found that to be a much better system

I've gone through a pretty insane dopamine detox over the last few months, and want to share some thoughts from the whole experience

The reason I wanted to do it was that my brain was utterly fried from the constant nonstop dopamine influx from social media, video games, junk food, netflix, email, and of course, the infinite online casino that is almost all of the crypto industry these days

It all felt incredibly unhealthy and unsustainable and while I didn't feel "unhappy", I did feel overwhelmed and like my brain was going to eventually explode if I kept going the way I was going

I'm not sure if it's just the way my brain works and if lots of people are able to adapt and run with this new world order we're finding ourselves in, or if this is some existential angst that is shared by most of the people reading this

But it really feels like things steamroll in one direction when it comes to dopamine and unless you're intentionally taking meaningful steps to protect yourself from the attacks, it's just gonna keep chipping away at your brain until you're forced to find some kind of reprieve

Personally, I stopped video games, deleted instagram and youtube from my phone, almost entirely stopped coming on X. I stopped watching TV, stopped scrolling feeds, stopped trading crypto, stopped sportsbetting or gambling.

The plan was to do it for 48-72hrs and then come back to reality, but that initial period was so blissful, I couldn't bring myself to come back.

Instead I stayed away. I checked in every now and then and kept up with some extremely basic work committments, and would occasionally watch a movie or something with the wife, but my screentime has basically been down 90%+ for the last 3 months

While a (big) part of me wishes I could stay like that forever, I also felt like I was missing something - the "productivity" lever of life. I had little projects I worked on, I played golf, I traveled, it was a utopian period really - anyone should be so lucky (and I am aware how lucky I am to have been able to take this time)

But it ultimately still left me feeling like I needed to come back to reality, to "work", to be a productive member of the world again - some way, some how

I'm not sure exactly what form that takes for me these days - I've tried so many things over the last couple of years, infinite pivots, and haven't quite found my lasting "thing" yet - if that's even a thing i'm gonna find. I've repeated some version of this cycle multiple times too - burnout, work hard, burnout, new idea, go hard, burnout, back to the memecoin trenches, burnout, launch new company, burnout, go all in on AI, burnout, burnout, burnout

I'm actually now sure what the point of this post is, now that I have gotten here. Maybe to tell everyone to take 2-3 days away from all the dopamine and rest your brains, see what it's like to live a life without technology for a bit

And that it is not "the answer". There is no "the answer" to any of this, we're all just rolling through life one day after another trying to figure it out, and no matter how utopian or good a certain lifestyle might seem, once you live it for a while, you'll usually find yourself wanting something else/different

Peace comes from within or something? Go figure, the monks had it right all along, and we all kinda know this deep down too - sometimes even explicitly - but sometimes we also need to be reminded of it again, and again, and again

I've gone through a pretty insane dopamine detox over the last few months, and want to share some thoughts from the whole experience

The reason I wanted to do it was that my brain was utterly fried from the constant nonstop dopamine influx from social media, video games, junk food, netflix, email, and of course, the infinite online casino that is almost all of the crypto industry these days

It all felt incredibly unhealthy and unsustainable and while I didn't feel "unhappy", I did feel overwhelmed and like my brain was going to eventually explode if I kept going the way I was going

I'm not sure if it's just the way my brain works and if lots of people are able to adapt and run with this new world order we're finding ourselves in, or if this is some existential angst that is shared by most of the people reading this

But it really feels like things steamroll in one direction when it comes to dopamine and unless you're intentionally taking meaningful steps to protect yourself from the attacks, it's just gonna keep chipping away at your brain until you're forced to find some kind of reprieve

Personally, I stopped video games, deleted instagram and youtube from my phone, almost entirely stopped coming on X. I stopped watching TV, stopped scrolling feeds, stopped trading crypto, stopped sportsbetting or gambling.

The plan was to do it for 48-72hrs and then come back to reality, but that initial period was so blissful, I couldn't bring myself to come back.

Instead I stayed away. I checked in every now and then and kept up with some extremely basic work committments, and would occasionally watch a movie or something with the wife, but my screentime has basically been down 90%+ for the last 3 months

While a (big) part of me wishes I could stay like that forever, I also felt like I was missing something - the "productivity" lever of life. I had little projects I worked on, I played golf, I traveled, it was a utopian period really - anyone should be so lucky (and I am aware how lucky I am to have been able to take this time)

But it ultimately still left me feeling like I needed to come back to reality, to "work", to be a productive member of the world again - some way, some how

I'm not sure exactly what form that takes for me these days - I've tried so many things over the last couple of years, infinite pivots, and haven't quite found my lasting "thing" yet - if that's even a thing i'm gonna find. I've repeated some version of this cycle multiple times too - burnout, work hard, burnout, new idea, go hard, burnout, back to the memecoin trenches, burnout, launch new company, burnout, go all in on AI, burnout, burnout, burnout

I'm actually now sure what the point of this post is, now that I have gotten here. Maybe to tell everyone to take 2-3 days away from all the dopamine and rest your brains, see what it's like to live a life without technology for a bit

And that it is not "the answer". There is no "the answer" to any of this, we're all just rolling through life one day after another trying to figure it out, and no matter how utopian or good a certain lifestyle might seem, once you live it for a while, you'll usually find yourself wanting something else/different

Peace comes from within or something? Go figure, the monks had it right all along, and we all kinda know this deep down too - sometimes even explicitly - but sometimes we also need to be reminded of it again, and again, and again
